SB-02.c01: An emergency can be a crash, a bus stalled on tracks or in a busy intersection, an engine fire, or a student who gets sick or hurt.
Knowing what to do **before, during and after** an evacuation can decide whether children live or die.
**Upwind** = the side the wind blows from, so smoke and fumes blow away from you.
**Containment (storage) area** = the space past the tracks where the whole bus can wait clear of the tracks.
**Tail swing** = the rear of the bus swinging out when you turn; a **lookout** warns you of danger while you back.
SB-02.c02: Step 1 is to **recognize the hazard**; if there is time, call your **dispatcher** and explain before you decide to evacuate.
Students are usually **safest on the bus**, unless staying puts them at needless risk; if you do evacuate, decide in time.
Weigh fire, leaking fuel, traffic, tornado or rising water, downed power lines, and whether moving students could worsen **neck or back injuries**.
You **must** evacuate for **5** reasons: fire or threat of fire, stalled on or next to a railroad crossing, bus position may change, imminent crash, HazMat spill.
SB-02.c03: When you can, assign **2 older, responsible students** to each emergency exit and another to lead students to a safe place; explain the plan to everyone.
Safe place: at least **100 ft** off the road, **toward oncoming traffic**; upwind of a fire; far from the tracks, toward the oncoming train.
Spilled HazMat: take students **upwind, at least 300 ft** from the bus.
Secure the bus (Park, parking brakes, engine off, key out, hazard lights) and **hang the mike out the window**; last resort for help: send **2** older students.
**Do not move** a possible neck or spine injury unless life is in immediate danger; afterward walk through the bus, **count** students, protect the scene.
SB-02.c04: **Passive crossing** = no traffic control device; you must stop, and the decision to cross is **entirely yours**.
**Active crossing** = flashing red lights (with or without bells), or flashing red lights with bells and **gates**.
The **advance warning sign** is **round, black on yellow**; pavement markings (an "X" with "RR") mean the same thing.
Keep the front of the bus behind a **white stop line**; with no white line, stop **before the crossbuck**.
Stop before the gate comes down; if it stays down after the train passes, never go around it — **call your dispatcher**.
SB-02.c05: In general, school buses **stop at all crossings**; a bus has no chance in a crash with a train.
Slow down, test your brakes, and turn on the **hazard lights about 200 ft** before the crossing; stay right and pick an escape route.
Stop **no closer than 15 ft** and **no farther than 50 ft** from the nearest rail, where you can see the tracks best.
While stopped: Park or Neutral, brakes set, radios off, passengers quiet, **service door and driver's window open**, then look and listen.
Multiple tracks: stop **only before the first**; cross in low gear without shifting; if the gate drops while you are crossing, **drive through it**.
SB-02.c06: Stalled or trapped on the tracks: get everyone off at once, moving away from the bus at an angle **away from the tracks and toward the train**.
Obey a police officer at the crossing; with no officer and a signal that seems broken, **call your dispatcher** and ask how to proceed.
Don't cross unless you can see far enough to be **certain** no train is coming; even when active signals show clear, still **look and listen**.
"If it will not fit, do not commit": space past the tracks = **bus length + 15 ft**, so a 40-ft bus needs 55 ft.
SB-02.c07: Don't handle behavior problems while **loading or unloading**; wait until the unloading students are safely off and away.
For serious problems, stop in a safe place **off the road**, secure the bus, **take the key** if you leave your seat, and speak firmly and respectfully.
If a seat change is needed, move the student to a seat **near you**.
**Never** put a student off the bus except **at school or their own stop**; if you cannot drive safely, call a school administrator or the police.
SB-02.c08: ABS is required on air-brake vehicles built on/after **March 1, 1998**, and on hydraulic-brake ones with GVWR 10,000 lb or more built on/after **March 1, 1999**.
ABS keeps the wheels from locking so you can **steer** while braking hard; a **yellow lamp** on the instrument panel warns of a malfunction.
Brake as you always have; in an emergency stop **do not pump** the brakes, and ease off as you slow to stay in control.
If ABS fails you still have **normal brakes**; get it serviced soon. An older system's lamp may stay on until you are going over **5 mph**.
ABS does **not** prevent power or turning skids, necessarily shorten stopping distance, or make up for bad brakes; the best safety feature is a safe driver.
SB-02.c09: Some school buses have a **white strobe light** on the roof, used when you cannot easily see around the bus.
[CA] Use the strobe **only** when visibility is **500 ft or less** because of fog, rain, snow, smoke, dust or similar conditions.
SB-02.c10: The side of a school bus works like a **sail**: strong wind can push it sideways, off the road, or even tip it over.
Grip the wheel **firmly** and expect gusts; **slow down** or pull off the road and wait, and call your dispatcher for advice.
SB-02.c11: Backing is **strongly discouraged**: do it only when there is no other safe way, and **never** when students are outside the bus.
[CA] You **may flash the hazard lights** while backing to warn drivers and people on foot.
Post a **lookout** who only warns you of obstacles, people and vehicles, not how to back; with no lookout, stop, take the keys and walk to the rear.
At a pick-up point **load first**, then back; at a drop-off point **back first**, then unload.
A school bus can have up to **3 ft** of tail swing, so check your mirrors before and during every turn.
